title: Find the stamp, copy the next word
allegory: An induction head is like a two-clerk filing trick: clerk one stamps every card with the word that came before it, and when a word shows up again, clerk two finds the card stamped with that word and copies whatever is written on it.
map: clerk one stamps each card with the word before it
the previous-token head (layer 0) writes 'the token before me was A' into position A+1
clerk two hunts for cards stamped with the current word
the induction head's query for A matches keys carrying that stamp: K-composition
copying the word written on the found card
the OV circuit copies the attended token B to the logits
the bright stripe in the attention picture
attention at offset 1 - seq_len on a repeated sequence
sack either clerk and the trick stops
ablating 0.7, 1.4 or 1.10 sends second-half loss back up
where_else: In-context learning: Olsson et al. (2022) tied a jump in it during training to induction heads forming
Copying names, code identifiers and repeated phrases from earlier in a prompt
The guess, detect, ablate loop you reuse for IOI, path patching and bracket classifiers
K-composition generally: any later head that looks where an earlier head's writing tells it to

hamming.what: A pair of attention heads that implement 'I saw A then B earlier, I'm at A again, so predict B'.
hamming.when: Whenever a sequence repeats something from earlier in its context, from random tokens to names and code.
hamming.why: It is the first circuit where two heads cooperate, it explains a visible jump in in-context learning during training, and its stripe gives a cheap detector you can check causally.

object.title: The stripe board
object.subtitle: Attention on a random five-word run shown twice: each row is a word looking back, each bar how hard it looks.

cap.1: An attention picture for a random five-word run, shown twice. Each row is a word looking back; the tall bars show where it looks.
cap.2: Induction head on [BOS, A..E, A..E]. Rows are destinations, columns are sources. Second-copy rows light up one step after the earlier copy.
cap.3: A stripe at offset 1 - seq_len = -4: destination i attends to i - 4, the token after the previous occurrence. First-copy rows rest on BOS.

cap.1: From above the stripe is plain: on the second pass every word looks at the word that followed it last time, and copies it.
cap.2: The induction score is the mean of this diagonal. Heads above about 0.4 count; in ARENA's two-layer model that is 1.4 and 1.10.
cap.3: Score = mean of pattern.diagonal(offset = 1 - seq_len), with seq_len the length of one copy and the BOS shift accounted for.

cap.1: Switch to clerk one, the previous-token head: every word simply looks one step back. That look is the stamping.
cap.2: The previous-token head (0.7 in ARENA's model) is a stripe at offset -1. It writes 'the token before me was A' into the next position.
cap.3: Offset -1 diagonal. Its output is what the induction head's keys read: K-composition across the two layers.

cap.1: A look-alike: the duplicate-token head looks back at the same word itself, one step too early to say what comes next.
cap.2: Duplicate-token head: offset -seq_len. It finds the earlier copy of the same token, not the token after it.
cap.3: Offset -seq_len = -5 here. Scoring at this offset instead of 1 - seq_len is the classic off-by-one detector bug.

cap.1: Sack clerk one and clerk two is lost: with no stamps to search for, the stripe vanishes and the model is back to guessing.
cap.2: Ablate the previous-token head and the induction stripe disappears, so second-half loss climbs back up.
cap.3: Zero-ablating 0.7 removes the key-side signal. That indirect effect is invisible to DLA, which is why ablation supplies the causal check.

predict.q: On the second copy of a repeated random sequence, where does an induction head at token A look?

options.t: At the token right after the earlier A
At the position just before it

predict.why: That token is what came next last time, so copying it predicts the next token. The earlier A itself is the duplicate-token head's target.

predict.q: You zero-ablate the layer-0 previous-token head. What happens to the induction stripe?

options.t: It fades: the keys lost their stamp
Nothing: the induction head works alone

predict.why: K-composition: the induction head's keys read what the previous-token head wrote.

predict.q: What does per-token loss look like on a repeated random sequence?

options.t: High on the first copy, low on the second

predict.why: Random tokens cannot be guessed the first time; the second time, the answer is already in the context.

object.where: Any lookup that keys on 'what came before' and returns 'what came next': names, code and repeated phrases.
